name: Nikhil Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the late shift mostly, so my day starts around two in the afternoon. I work for a care co-op in a seaside town, which means the carers own a share of it, and I do tea calls and bed calls from four until about ten at night. Mr Kowalski has Parkinson's, so I help him with his tea and his evening tablets, and he teaches me Polish words while I cook. Then a couple of bed calls, getting people changed and settled, and I'm home by half ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the co-op pays our travel time, which almost nobody else round here does. What wears me out is the money, still. I rent a room in a shared house near the harbour for most of what I earn, and I've had a six-hundred-pound overdraft for two years that never seems to shrink. Out of season there's not much other work in town either, just the chip shops and the caravan park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that care was never going to be done by a computer. I'd probably share a post on the co-op's page saying the real fight is still about pay and staff numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means not much changes, and that's not great news for me. I'm still on low pay with an overdraft, in a town where the jobs dry up every October. AI being hype doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my late shifts and maybe pick up an extra night sit a week to chip away at the overdraft. I use a chatbot now and then to translate things for Mr Kowalski, so I'd keep doing that. I'd also go to the co-op's members' meeting, because we're voting on pay this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, really. Not scared, just stuck. If AI is mostly hype, I'm still a twenty-seven-year-old carer with a six-hundred-pound overdraft in a town that empties every October.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the overdraft never shrinks. What eats the money each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent first, then the bus pass, food and my phone. I send my sister a bit sometimes when she's short. By the end of the month I'm back in the overdraft, every time, no matter what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the co-op itself feel safe to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, but the council contract is up for renewal next spring, and a big national agency is bidding against us. If we lost it, half of our clients would go. That's the thing that actually keeps me up, not AI.

say: I'd say care was never going to be done by a **computer**.
I'd post that the real fight is still about **pay** and staff numbers.
think: Not much changes, and that's **not great** for someone on low pay.
My **overdraft** and the town's dead winters stay exactly the same.
do: Pick up an **extra night sit** each week to chip away at the overdraft.
Keep using a **chatbot** to translate for Mr Kowalski now and then.
Vote at the co-op's **members' meeting** on pay this year.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, I'm still a twenty-seven-year-old carer with a six-hundred-pound overdraft in a town that empties every October.
fieldNote: Nikhil's real worry is the **council contract** renewal, not AI.
He sends money to his **sister** even while he's overdrawn.
He uses AI **casually** for translation, without any fuss.

steps.text: Take one extra night sit a week to pay off the overdraft
Vote for a pay rise at the co-op members' meeting
Keep the late shift of tea calls and bed calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, let AI do the forms, so we get more time with people. I'd push that line hard at the co-op, because we actually get a vote on how money's spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps the co-op compete with the big agencies, which might save my job. But it might also mean fewer office staff, and some of those are my friends. And the big agency would use it to undercut us even harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the group that picks any new software, because we're a co-op and members can do that. I'd learn the tool once a few others had tried it, maybe the care notes one. I'd keep doing the extra night sit and keep paying the overdraft down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Hopeful for the co-op, worried for Jodie and Pete in the office. AI writing the care notes could save my co-op, or it could help the big agency undercut us. I honestly can't tell which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your job are thinking work that AI could take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes I write after each call, the medication chart, and texting the office when someone's not right. That's maybe a quarter of my time. The rest is cooking, washing, lifting and talking, and no software does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools if the co-op brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, once a few people had shown me it works. I already use one to translate for Mr Kowalski, so I'm not scared of it. I just don't want to be the first one who gets it wrong.

say: I'd say let AI do the **forms** so carers get more time with people.
I'd push that line at the **co-op**, where members get a vote.
think: AI could help the co-op **compete** with the big agencies.
It might also cut **office staff**, and some of them are my friends.
do: Join the co-op group that **picks software** for care notes.
Learn the **notes tool** once a few colleagues have tried it.
Keep the **extra night sit** and keep paying down the overdraft.
feel: **Hopeful** for the co-op but **worried** for Jodie and Pete in the office.
S1.quote: AI writing the care notes could save my co-op, or it could help the big agency undercut us. I honestly can't tell which.
fieldNote: Nikhil sees AI as both a **lifeline** and a weapon for the competition.
About a **quarter** of his time is thinking work like notes and charts.
He'll adopt tools once **proven** by colleagues, not before.

steps.text: Join the co-op working group choosing care-notes software
Learn the care-notes app after colleagues have tested it
Keep the extra weekly night sit for overdraft payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership of care, and I'd mean it. I'd be on every co-op and union call saying robots in homes have to be decided by carers and families, not tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it means I've got until about 2031 and then I'm in trouble. Thinking AI in 2028 hits the office and the paperwork, which I can live with. But the hands-on work is everything I do, and robots three years later would take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now, clearing the overdraft as fast as I could, even if it meant two night sits a week. I'd join the national care union as well as the co-op, because one small co-op can't fight this alone. By 2031 I'd want some kind of training lined up, maybe something with kids, where parents might still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting. Two years for thinking AI and five for robots means I'd be thirty-one and starting again from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between thinking AI and robots look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy, maybe. The co-op would cut office jobs and dump some work onto us, but they'd still need hands on the ground. I'd be using whatever tools they gave me and trying not to think about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most worried about in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Kowalski, honestly. He's lonely, and his son lives in Leeds. If a robot did his tea, nobody would be there to teach Polish words to, and that's half of why he gets up.

say: I'd say this is why we need **public ownership** of care.
I'd argue **carers and families** should decide on robots in homes, not tech firms.
think: I've got until about **2031**, then the hands-on work goes.
Thinking AI in 2028 hits the **office**, which I could live with.
do: Do **two night sits** a week to clear the overdraft fast.
Join the **national care union** as well as the co-op.
Line up **training** with children's services before 2031.
S2.quote: Two years for thinking AI and five for robots means I'd be thirty-one and starting again from nothing.
fieldNote: Nikhil reads the **robot gap** clearly: three years, then his core work goes.
His first worry is for **Mr Kowalski**, a lonely client, not himself.
He'd move toward **children's work**, guessing parents would still want people.

steps.text: Do two night sits a week to clear the overdraft
Join the national care workers' union alongside the co-op
Look into training for work with children before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that carers and families should decide this. With five years I'd also say the government should pay for carers to retrain, not just wave us goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years feels more manageable. It's 2034 before robots do the hands-on work, so I'd be thirty-five, which is still young. I'd have time to clear the overdraft and maybe do a course part time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the overdraft in the first year with the extra night sits. Then I'd do an evening course, maybe teaching assistant, starting in 2028 or so. I'd also use AI tools more at work, once the co-op had them, so I'm not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not panicked. With five years I could clear my overdraft and get a teaching assistant course done before any robot reaches my clients' kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years instead of two change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between running and walking. With two years I'm grabbing at anything. With five I can pick something and actually finish it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents or sister say about you retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister would say go for it, she's always said I'm wasted in care. Mum would worry about the money, because she always does. I'd probably ask them both for a bit of help with the course fees.

say: I'd say carers and families should **decide** on robots in care.
I'd call on the government to **pay for retraining** for carers.
think: Robots in **2034** means I'd be thirty-five, which is still young.
Five years feels **manageable** for clearing debt and a part-time course.
do: Clear the **overdraft** in the first year with extra night sits.
Start an **evening course** as a teaching assistant around 2028.
Use the co-op's **AI tools** more once they arrive.
S3.quote: With five years I could clear my overdraft and get a teaching assistant course done before any robot reaches my clients' kitchens.
fieldNote: Nikhil describes the extra time as the difference between **running and walking**.
He'd ask his **sister** and mum to help with course fees.
His plan has a real order: **debt first**, then a course.

steps.text: Clear the six-hundred-pound overdraft in the first year
Start an evening teaching assistant course around 2028
Use the co-op's AI note tools once they arrive
Ask Mum and his sister to help with course fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want the co-op to start planning now for how robots and carers work side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think with ten years I'd be fine. I'd have the overdraft gone, a qualification done, and maybe a job that mixes care and something else. I'd be forty when the robots come, and I'd want to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the overdraft, then maybe save a bit for once. I'd do a part-time qualification over a few years, maybe occupational therapy assistant, helping people relearn how to do things. I'd keep using AI tools at work as they become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Almost calm, to be honest. Ten years is long enough for me to train properly, and short enough that I can't keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still leave care at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. If I became an occupational therapy assistant, I'd still be in care, just a different bit of it. That's what I'd want, really, to stay with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op look like in 2039, in your best guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller team of carers, each one working with a robot or two for the lifting and the night checks. The carers would do the talking, the planning and the hard calls. I'd want to be one of them, or training them.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** we shouldn't waste.
I'd want the co-op to plan for robots and carers **side by side**.
think: With ten years I'd probably be **fine**, debt gone and qualified.
I'd be **forty** when the robots come and want to be ready.
do: Clear the overdraft, then **save a bit** for once.
Train part time as an **occupational therapy assistant** over a few years.
Keep using **AI tools** at work as they become normal.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to train properly, and short enough that I can't keep putting it off.
fieldNote: Ten years turns Nikhil from alarmed to **uneasy**, with a clear plan.
He'd stay **in care** through occupational therapy, not leave it.
He imagines carers working **alongside robots** and wants to train them.

steps.text: Build a small savings pot once the overdraft is gone
Train part time as an occupational therapy assistant
Use AI note tools at the co-op as they become normal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come before I'd cleared my debts or trained for anything. What would help is free retraining for carers and the co-op keeping the council contract. Give carers a decent wage and a fair shot at training, and most of us will work out the robot part ourselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what clients want. Mr Kowalski says he'd rather have a robot than a different stranger every night. That stuck with me, because the big agencies already send strangers.

headlineQuote: Give carers a decent wage and a fair shot at training, and most of us will work out the robot part ourselves.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old** late-shift carer at a seaside care co-op that pays travel time.
He rents a room near the harbour and carries a **six-hundred-pound overdraft**.
He uses AI **now and then**, mostly to translate for Mr Kowalski, a client with Parkinson's.
He swings from **alarmed** under AGI in two years to uneasy with ten.
His answer is **debt first**, then training, while staying close to care work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive before he'd cleared debts or trained.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op keeping its **council contract** next spring.
